name: Cranberry
lede: Cranberry is a deep crimson-red named for the fruit.

sections.title: The fruit's name
sections.body:
Paterson lists cranberry red as the dark red of the cranberry, and gives it a place in his red column beside cramoisy, crimson and damson [1][2]. St Clair, describing pomegranate, reaches for the same fruit and calls it cranberry-pink, which shows how loosely the word is used [3]. Where the word was first coined as a color is undocumented in the books here [1][3].

The swatch is #9E003A, ISCC-NBS block 13 and also a survey name from the xkcd color list [4]. A second swatch called Cranberry, #9C2542, cites Crayola and sits within 2.3 units of a red-violet on a color wheel [4]. So the name points at a band of deep reds with a violet cast, not one fixed color [4].

sections.title: Where it sits
sections.body:
The nearest named color is [[raspberry]], 4.3 units away [4]. Other deep reds in our library include [[cherry]], [[burgundy]] and [[blood-red]] [4].

The swatch on a screen is a saturated crimson, and the fruit itself is likely duller [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a rare color in painting. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, only one work has a color within six units of this swatch covering at least five per cent of the canvas [5]. It is Kirchner's *Two Girls under an Umbrella* of 1910, at 13 per cent [[painting:nga-76206|Two Girls under an Umbrella]] [5]. The one hit is German and dated 1910 [5].

The same sample returns zero hits from the Impressionists and the Realists [5]. In Google Books, the word *cranberry* is present from 1800 and peaks about 1925, but that count is mostly about the fruit [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read the match as a screen color [5].
